stem: A 65-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with persistent chest discomfort at rest for the last 45 minutes. His ECG shows no ST-segment elevation, but his high-sensitivity troponin-I is significantly elevated. He is started on aspirin and anticoagulation. Coronary angiography shows a partially occluded coronary artery with reduced distal flow. Based on these findings, which diagnosis best explains his condition?
stemHtml: A 65-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with persistent chest discomfort at rest for the last 45 minutes. His ECG shows no ST-segment elevation, but his high-sensitivity troponin-I is significantly elevated. He is started on aspirin and anticoagulation. Coronary angiography shows a partially occluded coronary artery with reduced distal flow. Based on these findings, which diagnosis best explains his condition? (Question Id: 502122)
options: STEMI due to complete transmural infarction
keywords: 1. “No ST-segment elevation” → Immediately rules out STEMI and Prinzmetal angina (which shows ST elevation during pain).
2. “Troponin significantly elevated” → Indicates myocardial necrosis → distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina or stable angina.
3. “Partially occluded coronary artery” → Fits NSTEMI mechanism (incomplete occlusion → subendocardial infarction).
keywordsHtml: 1. “No ST-segment elevation” → Immediately rules out STEMI and Prinzmetal angina (which shows ST elevation during pain).
2. “Troponin significantly elevated” → Indicates myocardial necrosis → distinguishes NSTEMI from unstable angina or stable angina.
3. “Partially occluded coronary artery” → Fits NSTEMI mechanism (incomplete occlusion → subendocardial infarction).

E.title: NSTEMI due to subendocardial ischemia
E.body:
The patient has ischemic chest pain at rest + elevated troponin + NO ST elevation → this is the classic diagnostic triad of NSTEMI.
Coronary angiography shows partial occlusion, which causes subendocardial (not full-thickness) ischemia.
STEMI requires complete occlusion and ST elevation, which are absent here.
NSTEMI pathophysiology: plaque rupture → incomplete thrombotic occlusion → necrosis limited to subendocardium.
The resultant ischemia in NSTEMI is typically confined to the subendocardium, the layer of the heart muscle most vulnerable to oxygen deprivation.
E.bodyHtml:
• The patient has ischemic chest pain at rest + elevated troponin + NO ST elevation → this is the classic diagnostic triad of NSTEMI.
  • Coronary angiography shows partial occlusion, which causes subendocardial (not full-thickness) ischemia.
  • STEMI requires complete occlusion and ST elevation, which are absent here.
  • NSTEMI pathophysiology: plaque rupture → incomplete thrombotic occlusion → necrosis limited to subendocardium.
  • The resultant ischemia in NSTEMI is typically confined to the subendocardium, the layer of the heart muscle most vulnerable to oxygen deprivation.

A.title: Prinzmetal Angina
A.body:
Caused by coronary vasospasm, producing transient ST elevation during pain.
Troponin is usually normal, and coronary arteries are typically clean between episodes.
Doesn’t match the elevated troponin and partial occlusion.
A.bodyHtml:
• Caused by coronary vasospasm, producing transient ST elevation during pain.
  • Troponin is usually normal, and coronary arteries are typically clean between episodes.
  • Doesn’t match the elevated troponin and partial occlusion.

B.title: Myocarditis
B.body:
Often presents after viral illness with global ECG changes, not localized ischemic changes.
Troponin can rise, but coronary angiography is usually normal, not showing partial occlusion.
Chest pain may occur, but the angiographic findings don't fit.
B.bodyHtml:
• Often presents after viral illness with global ECG changes, not localized ischemic changes.
  • Troponin can rise, but coronary angiography is usually normal, not showing partial occlusion.
  • Chest pain may occur, but the angiographic findings don't fit.

C.title: Stable Angina
C.body:
Pain is predictable, exertional, and relieved by rest; never causes troponin elevation.
No rest pain lasting 45 minutes, and no biomarker leak.
Stable angina → normal troponin, by definition.
C.bodyHtml:
• Pain is predictable, exertional, and relieved by rest; never causes troponin elevation.
  • No rest pain lasting 45 minutes, and no biomarker leak.
  • Stable angina → normal troponin, by definition.

D.title: STEMI due to complete transmural infarction
D.body:
Requires complete occlusion + ST elevation on ECG.
This patient has no ST elevation and only partial occlusion, so STEMI is ruled out.
D.bodyHtml:
• Requires complete occlusion + ST elevation on ECG.
  • This patient has no ST elevation and only partial occlusion, so STEMI is ruled out.

keyConcept: NSTEMI occurs due to incomplete coronary artery occlusion, producing subendocardial ischemia with elevated troponin but no ST elevation. Coronary angiography typically shows partial obstruction, distinguishing it from STEMI and stable angina.

diagrams.heading: Acute Coronary Syndrome NSTEMI (Non–ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction)
diagrams.description: This diagram illustrates the pathophysiology of NSTEMI, showing atherosclerotic plaque rupture leading to partial coronary artery occlusion and resulting in subendocardial ischemia and myocardial necrosis. It highlights key clinical features such as chest pain at rest, diagnostic findings including elevated troponin without ST elevation on ECG, and outlines core management strategies like antiplatelets, anticoagulation, and early invasive intervention.
